context: Wilde to Frank Harris, 21 November 1900, Hotel d'Alsace - nine days before his death. He is demanding the 175 pounds Harris undertook in his own handwriting to pay within a week, two months earlier, for Mr and Mrs Daventry. The friendship is audibly strained: 'I do not wish to criticise your conduct towards me, I merely state the plain facts.'
quote: Dear Frank, I have now been in bed for nearly ten weeks and am still extremely ill, having had a relapse a fortnight ago. I must, however, for many reasons write to you at once on the question of the money you owe me. The expenses of my illness amount to close on £200 and I must beg that you pay me immediately the sum for which you are still indebted to me. On September 26th, nearly two months ago, you drew up an agreement in your own handwriting promising to pay me within a week from that date the sum of £175 besides one-fourth of all profits. You explained to me that you had left your cheque-book in London, but that you would ~~return~~ send me a cheque on your return, which was fixed for the following day. You gave me £25 on account and I naturally accepted the word of one of my oldest friends, backed up by an agreement drawn out by himself, not actually signed, but I gave you a receipt for the entire sum. I no more doubted that you would pay me in the course of a week, than I doubted of the shining of sun or moon. A week passed over without my hearing a line from you and finally the surgeon felt it his duty to inform me that unless I was operated on immediately it would be too late and that the consequences of the delay would probably be fatal. With great difficulty I managed to raise amongst my friends, or rather the sum was raised for me by them, the 1500 francs which was the surgeon's fee, and was duly operated on under chloroform. I then telegraphed to you to ask you to send the money you owed me at once. All I received from you in return was £25. You then took no further notice of the matter but left me for a whole month in the most terrible position I have ever been in. I do not wish to criticise your conduct towards me, I merely state the plain facts. You owe at present, on your agreement of two months ago, the sum of £125. You also owe me £25 additional, my share of the £100 paid over in advance by Mrs Campbell. You told me at Durand's that this sum was not in advance of fees. I should like to know whether this is the case or not. The play has now been running for, I believe, three weeks and I have received no account of the receipts or royalties. A statement of the receipts and my proportion of authors' fees should, of course, be sent to me every week. I must ask you to at once settle up accounts as I cannot possibly go on living in the present manner, with two doctors and attendants, a medical nurse and all the terrible expenses incident on a long and dangerous illness. With regard to Smithers, I am, I need hardly say, astounded that you should have allowed yourself to be blackmailed by him, but your proposal to recoup yourself out of the money you owe me and to sequestrate my small share of the profits, is of course out of the question. I could not allow it for a moment. Smithers had an agreement with me some years ago to write him a play within a certain given time. I was unable to carry out my side of the agreement, and Smithers formally relinquished to me in Paris any claim he had on me for the broken agreement. It is true I did not get Smithers’ pronunciation in writing, but Smithers was at that time a great friend of mine, and in his case, as later on in yours, I considered the word of a friend adequate. I promised him in return to give him the publishing rights of two of my plays, as well as the copyright of a poem for which illustrations were at that time being made by an artist of great ability. Since that time Smithers, as you know, has become bankrupt & I am one of his creditors. Had Smithers considered [inserted: that] his agreement with me was still valid he would naturally have entered it as an asset against me, but he did not do so, showing clearly that the agreement in his opinion had lapsed in realy as it had lapsed in time. His coming to you and attempting to extort money from you is really an act of blackmailing, for if my lapsed agreement with him has the value of five shillings, it belongs of course to the Official Receiver, and Smithers has no more right to deal with it or treat it as his property than the man in the street. It is unnecessary to tell you, I presume, that what Smithers has done is a most serious offence against the bankruptcy laws, and if it came to the knowledge of the Official Receiver, Smithers would find himself in a very painful, possibly criminal position. If you will put these facts before your lawyer he will tell you that I am perfectly right. And I should fancy that unless Smithers has spent the £100 he extorted from you in whiskeys and sodas, your solicitor will be able to recover the money for you. However that is your business, not mine, but as Smithers is having a very bad time with the Official Receiver, I should not fancy that he would care to risk imprisonment. When the man Nethersole intruded here almost daily during the worst crisis of my illness and tried to blackmail me on the ground that he had managed to secure a copy of the scenario & that a play belonged to any man who had a copy of the scenario, if under these circumstances I had been foolish enough to hand him £200, I think you would have been rather amused if I had written subsequently to you to claim the £200 from your pocket. But, without adducing parallels, your lawyer will tell you that Smithers’s action is entirely illegal, and that you were very foolish to yield to it for a moment. As for me, I regret what has occurred for your sake, but I cannot recoup you, nor should you for a moment expect me to do so. The important thing, however, is to settle up our accounts & I must beg you to send me by return the £150 you owe me as well as any royalties that may be due. I need not say how distressed I am that things should have turned out in this manner between us, but you must remember that the fault is in no sense mine; had you kept your word to me, fulfilled the agreement & sent me the money that was due to me & for which I gave you a receipt which you still hold, all would have been well; and indeed I myself would have perfectly recovered two weeks ago had it not been for the state of mental anxiety which your conduct kept me in all day long, with its accompanying sleeplessness at night, a sleeplessness over which none of the opiates the doctors dared to order me seemed to have any effect. Today is Tuesday the 20th. I rely on receiving from you the £150 you owe me. Sincerely yours Oscar Wilde
original_provenance: Read at HRC MSS_WildeO_2_6_003 to _010, eight sides, the sheets numbered 2 and 3 by the writer on _006 and _009. Two hands, and this governs how the marks are read. The volume's footnote says 'Except for the last two lines, this letter is in the hand of Maurice Gilbert', and the scans bear it out: _003 to _009 are a neat regular hand that is not Wilde's, _010 is unmistakably his - smaller, spikier, sloping. On the images the change looks to come earlier than the last two lines but the transition is not resolvable at this resolution, so the footnote stands. Emphasis: none - nothing is underlined on any of the eight sides, a null finding. Cancellations: the body carries about nine, all of them an amanuensis correcting himself mid-copy - '~~return~~ send me a cheque' on _004 is the clearest, and there is a caret insertion of 'that' on _006. These are GILBERT'S, not Wilde's, and must not be read as Wilde striking anything out; only the cancelled word kept in the quotation is 'return', which changes the sense of the sentence. Elisions, now closed: the three passages this entry used to elide - Smithers's bankruptcy and the Nethersole blackmail - are restored in full. They were elided because the text mirror rendered them too poorly to trust; they were recovered by rendering pp. 1207 of the printed volume and reading it, which is also how the letter's true extent came out. It runs pp. 1206-1208, not p. 1206. Text corrections from the same render: the earlier quote here was mirror-derived and carried at least four errors, none of them visible without the page - 'not entirely signed, but gave you a receipt' for 'not actually signed, but I gave you a receipt'; 'I cannot reason' for 'I cannot recoup you'; 'the opium the doctors dared to order me' for 'the opiates'; and a missing 'Oscar Wilde' under 'Sincerely yours'. Collated against the sheets, images 6 to 8. The words of the two restored passages match the printed page exactly. What the page does not show, and is now carried here: Gilbert writes '&' for 'and' at least twice ('bankrupt & I am one of his creditors', 'scenario & that a play belonged'), which the volume expands; he writes 'Smithers'' where the volume prints 'Smithers's'; and he writes 'lapsed in realy' for 'reality', which the volume silently corrects. Three further cancellations, all his and all mid-copy slips: a struck word before 'on me for the broken agreement'; 'what ~~Smithers~~ has done'; and 'to secure ~~the~~ a copy of the scenario'. None is in the volume. The caret insertion, '[inserted: that]' after 'Had Smithers considered', is on image 6. One place where the edition may be supplying rather than reading: at 'for if my lapsed agreement with has the value of five shillings' the sheet appears to lack the word the volume prints as 'him'. Not corrected here in either direction; the gap is noted and the volume's reading left in the quote. Punctuation generally: Gilbert punctuates sparsely, running clauses together with no comma at all, and the volume adds commas throughout. Those are not reproduced comma by comma - the amanuensis's pointing is not Wilde's and reproducing it would imply a fidelity the document cannot carry. What is reproduced is every place the sheet says something different, rather than merely less. Date: the heading on _003 reads '21st Nov. 1900', matching the volume; Wilde's own close on _010 says 'Today is Tuesday the 20th'. 20 November 1900 was a Tuesday.
